,Below is a step-by-step checklist you can run locally to **(1) discover the layer names that are inside the archive** and **(2) make sure the file is structurally sound** before you push it to S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, etc.
The CLI is a single binary – no npm, no Python, no Docker required.
| macOS (Intel/Apple Silicon) | `brew install pmtiles`  *(Homebrew now ships the latest release)* |

| Linux (amd64/arm64) | Download the tarball from the latest GitHub release:
`curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v1.12.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64.tar.gz | tar xz` |
| Windows | Grab `pmtiles-windows-amd64.exe` from the same releases page and rename it to `pmtiles.exe`. |
| Docker (any platform) | `docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/data protomaps/go-pmtiles:latest <command>` – just prepend `docker run …` to the commands below. |
> **Tip:** Put the binary on your `$PATH` (e.g. `~/bin`) so you can call `pmtiles` from any folder.
- **Zoom range** (`Min zoom` / `Max zoom`) – MapLibre will automatically use these when you reference the source with `url:`.
- **Bounds** – useful for checking that the file really covers the area you expect.
- **Tile count** – sanity-check that the file isn’t empty.
If any of those numbers look wrong (e.g. `Max zoom: 0`), you probably generated the archive with the wrong `-z`/`--maxzoom` flag and need to re-run the tile generator.
## 3️⃣ Get the **layer list** (the names you will use in `source-layer`)
The layer names live in the JSON metadata under the `vector_layers` array. You have to ask the CLI to dump the full metadata:
**What to copy:** The `id` values (`water`, `roads`, `buildings`, `landuse`). Those are exactly the strings you will put in each layer’s `""source-layer""` property in your MapLibre style.

> **Common mistake:** Looking at the plain `pmtiles show` output (without `--metadata`) and not seeing the layer list. The plain output only prints non-string metadata as `<object, use --metadata to view full JSON metadata>`. Always add `--metadata` when you need the layer names.
The `verify` sub-command walks the file, checks offsets, tile counts, header consistency, and makes sure the internal index is sorted correctly.
- **Success:** The command exits with status 0 and prints `✅ verification succeeded`.

- **Failure:** It prints an error line such as `❌ tile offset out of bounds at z=12 x=345 y=678`. The exit code will be non-zero, so you can use it in CI pipelines (`pmtiles verify … && echo ""OK""`).
Run this **after every conversion** (`pmtiles convert …`) or after you run `pmtiles extract` to make a regional subset. If `verify` fails, re-run the conversion or extraction

negative — wrong tool for live PostGIS data,skills/maplibre-pmtiles-patterns/SKILL.md,"I'm building a map that shows bus positions updating every 30 seconds from a PostGIS database. Should I use PMTiles?

,**Short answer:** No – PMTiles is a *static* archive format. It’s perfect for serving a fixed set of tiles (basemaps, historic layers, raster imagery, etc.) without a tile-server, but it cannot reflect data that changes every 30 seconds. For live bus positions you’ll want a source that can be queried on demand (or pushed) from your PostGIS database.
## Why PMTiles Won’t Work for Real-Time Bus Data

| **Data mutability** | Immutable once the file is written. You would have to rebuild and re-upload the whole archive each time the data changes – impractical for a 30 s cadence. | Data lives in a database
column2: you can query the latest positions on every request (or push updates). |

column1: | **Delivery model** | Single file served via HTTP range requests. The client only reads the bytes that already exist in the archive. | Needs a server (or API) that can generate a fresh tile/feature set for the current timestamp. |
| **Cache-ability** | Long-term caching is a benefit (the file never changes). | You want *short* cache times (or no cache) so the map shows the newest positions. |
| **Complexity** | Zero-ops after upload – great for basemaps. | Requires a tile-server, a GeoJSON endpoint, or a WebSocket push layer to keep the map fresh. |
Because the bus layer is constantly changing, the “single-file, static-only” nature of PMTiles makes it a mismatch.
## Recommended Approaches for a 30-second-updated Bus Layer
| Option | How it works | Pros | Cons |

| **Martin** (MapLibre’s lightweight tile server) | `martin serve` can read a PostGIS table and serve vector tiles on the fly (`/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`). | Very little code, works with MapLibre out-of-the-box, supports CORS, can be run on a cheap VM or container. | Still a server process to maintain. |

| **tileserver-gl** (or **tileserver-php**, **t-rex**, **tegola**) | Same idea – a small HTTP service that reads PostGIS and returns vector tiles (or GeoJSON). | Mature, many examples, can also serve raster, sprites, glyphs. | Slightly heavier than Martin, more configuration. |

| **Custom Express/Go/FastAPI endpoint** | Write an endpoint that runs a SQL query (`SELECT * FROM bus_positions WHERE updated_at > now() - interval '30 seconds'`) and returns GeoJSON or MVT. | Full control, can add authentication, filtering, clustering, etc. | You have to implement tile generation (e.g., using `@mapbox/vector-tile`, `geojson-vt`, `tippecanoe`-style pipelines). |
// Example using a vector tile endpoint
// OR, if the server implements TileJSON:
'source-layer': 'bus_positions',   // name of the layer inside the MVT
*Important:* Use the **`tiles:`** template (or a TileJSON `url:`) rather than a PMTiles `url:` because the server is generating tiles per request.
If the number of buses is modest (a few hundred) you can skip tiles altogether:
- < 5 k features total (MapLibre can handle a few thousand points comfortably).
- You want the simplest stack (no tile server).
- You don’t need the level-of-detail benefits of vector tiles (e.g., clustering at low zoom).
For truly real-time feel (sub-second latency) you can push updates from the backend:
1. Backend watches the `bus_positions` table (e.g., via `LISTEN/NOTIFY` in PostgreSQL).
2. When a position changes, it sends a small JSON payload over a WebSocket.
3. Client updates the GeoJSON source with `setData` or `setFeatureState`.
This approach still uses a **GeoJSON source** on the client, but the data arrives as soon as it changes, eliminating the 30-second poll.
You can keep a **PMTiles basemap** (roads, landuse, etc.) for the background and combine it with any of the live-data methods above for the bus overlay.
// Live bus overlay (choose one of the methods above)
This gives you the performance and low-ops benefits of PMTiles for the static layers while still delivering real-time bus positions.
## Quick Checklist – Do *not* use PMTiles for this use-case
- ❌ Data changes every 30 s → PMTiles would need to be regenerated and re-uploaded each cycle.
- ❌ You need short cache times / no caching → PMTiles are usually cached for months.
- ❌ You want per-request filtering (e.g., only buses in the current viewport) → a tile server can do that

anti-pattern — tiles array template bypasses PMTiles header zoom range,skills/maplibre-pmtiles-patterns/SKILL.md,"I wired my PMTiles source with a tiles array (pmtiles://.../{z}/{x}/{y}) instead of url, and past a certain zoom the tiles go blank. The file is fine in pmtiles show. Why?

column2: DR

column1: You used the **`tiles:`** property (a URL template) to point at a `.pmtiles` file:

When the map reaches a zoom level that is **higher than the archive’s own `maxzoom`**, MapLibre keeps asking for tiles that simply don’t exist in the file. Because the request is made to a URL that contains `{z}/{x}/{y}`, MapLibre can’t read the PM-Tiles header to learn the real zoom range, so it assumes the default `maxzoom: 22`. The result is a series of **blank tiles** (or “no data” tiles) after the archive’s max-zoom.

The fix is to use **`url:`** (or supply the correct `maxzoom` yourself). With `url:` the PMTiles protocol reads the archive header, returns a proper TileJSON, and MapLibre automatically knows the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom` and will over-zoom gracefully.
| Property | What MapLibre does | Why it matters for PMTiles |

| **`url:`** (e.g. `pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles`) | Calls the PMTiles protocol handler → reads the archive header → returns a TileJSON that contains `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `bounds`, `vector_layers`, etc. | The client now knows the exact zoom range that the file actually contains. If you ask for zoom > `maxzoom`, MapLibre will **over-zoom** (reuse the highest-available tiles) instead of requesting non-existent tiles. |

| **`tiles:`** (template) | Treats the string as a normal XYZ tile URL template. No special handler is invoked for the header. | MapLibre falls back to the default `maxzoom: 22`. When you zoom past the archive’s real max-zoom, it asks the server for tiles that are not in the file → the PMTiles library returns an empty response → the map shows blanks. |
### Why the blank tiles appear only *after* a certain zoom
1. **Archive’s max-zoom** (e.g. 14) is stored in the PMTiles header.
2. You reference the file with `tiles:` → MapLibre thinks the source can serve up to zoom 22.
3. Zoom 0-14 → tiles exist → they are fetched via HTTP range requests and rendered correctly.
5. The PMTiles library looks for those tiles inside the file, finds none, and returns an empty buffer → MapLibre draws a blank tile.
If you inspect the network panel you’ll see 200 OK responses with **zero-byte bodies** (or a tiny “no-tile” response) for those high-zoom requests.

No `tiles:` array, no manual `maxzoom` needed – the PMTiles protocol does the heavy lifting.
